fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says to make “…an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense.” It's right there in the very first verse, so no digging required. Aaron burns the incense every morning and again at twilight (Exodus 30:7-8). Once a year he also makes atonement on its horns (Exodus 30:10).

Grain offering is a fair guess, but it's not what God says. He says this altar is for burning incense. Then He says, “…you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering…” on it (Exodus 30:9). So grain offerings are named as something that doesn't go here.

I see why you'd pick it, since offerings come up all through these plans. But God says this altar is for the burning of incense. He even says, "nor are you to pour a drink offering on it." (Exodus 30:9). Nothing gets poured on this one.

No elders in this verse, baker. Not one folding chair set out for them. God says the altar goes “…where I will meet with you.” That's Him talking to Moses, Israel's leader, and the gathering He describes is God meeting with him.

True! God says Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), “…must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come.” He lights it at the morning and again at twilight (Exodus 30:7-8). Generations to come? That's a longer run than any batch I've ever baked.

It's actually true. God says Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), “…must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come.” So the burning isn't a one-week project. It goes on for generations.

This one's false, friend. God says, “On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering…” That's a plain no on burnt offerings. This altar is for burning incense, and once a year Aaron makes atonement on its horns (Exodus 30:10).

Nope, no army supplies here, baker. A war chest sounds very official for a census, I'll give you that. But God tells Moses to take the atonement money “…and use it for the service of the Tent of Meeting.” That's where it goes, and soldiers don't come up in these verses.

That's a kind guess, friend. But God doesn't say that in these verses. He says to use the atonement money “…for the service of the Tent of Meeting.” He does say the rich shall not give more than a half shekel and the poor shall not give less (Exodus 30:15), but where the money goes is the Tent of Meeting.

That's right, baker! The basin is for Aaron and his sons, who are to wash their hands and feet in it. God says to set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar and put water in it. A basin of water for hands and feet, and it carries a serious instruction. Whenever they enter the Tent or approach the altar, they must wash (Exodus 30:20).

Drinking is a fair guess, but not here. God says the water is for Aaron and his sons “…to wash their hands and feet.” Nobody is filling a cup at this basin in these verses. Hands and feet are what the water is for.

You got it, baker. God says, “…they must wash with water so that they will not die.” He says it again in verse 21. He also calls it “…a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants for the generations to come.” That's serious business, and it's worth slowing down for.

That one's true, friend. God says to consecrate these things “…so that they will be most holy,” and then adds, “Whatever touches them shall be holy.” That's a lot of holy in one verse. I'd wipe off my mustache before I went reaching near any of it.

Judges is a fair guess, but it's not the word here. God says to anoint Aaron and his sons “…and consecrate them to serve Me as priests.” Judges isn't in this verse at all. Priests is what fills the blank.
